confidence_note: Easily confused with Hemlock (Conium maculatum), which is extremely toxic. Always check for plain green stems and no smell.
summary: Tall, lacy white-flowered plant that foams along hedgerows and roadsides in spring. One of the most abundant wildflowers of the English countryside — and easily confused with the deadly Hemlock.
full_description: Cow Parsley (Anthriscus sylvestris) creates frothy white drifts along hedgerows, field margins, and woodland edges from April to June. Reaching 40–100cm tall, it has hollow green stems (never purple-blotched), finely divided feathery leaves in a triangular outline, and flat-topped white flower heads (umbels) — each a compound of smaller umbrellas branching from the central stem. The plant has no distinctive smell when leaves are crushed, which is an important contrast with the similar-looking but extremely toxic Hemlock. Cow Parsley belongs to the carrot family (Apiaceae), named for the characteristic umbrella-shaped flower heads. It is a biennial or short-lived perennial, dying back in winter and re-emerging vigorously in spring from a taproot.
danger_note: The plant itself is harmless, but it closely resembles Hemlock (Conium maculatum), which is extremely toxic. Cow Parsley has plain green stems and no smell. Hemlock has purple-blotched hollow stems and a musty unpleasant smell. Never eat any white-flowered umbellifer without expert verification.
native_info: Native throughout the UK and common in most habitats, particularly in fertile soils along roadsides, hedgerows, and woodland edges.
wildlife_value: An important early food source for many insects. The open flower structure makes nectar easily accessible to hoverflies, beetles, and small bees. Several moth species use Cow Parsley as a larval food plant, and hollow dead stems provide nesting sites for solitary bees over winter.

life_stages.description: In early spring, Cow Parsley emerges with fresh bright green feathery leaves. Already recognisable by its distinctive finely divided, triangular leaf shape at 10–30cm tall. The stems are distinctly hollow and plain green — look closely and you can see they are not solid. No flowers yet, but the plant is growing rapidly in the warming hedgerow.

The iconic white flower heads appear in spring, creating lacy clouds along hedgerows. Each flower cluster is a flat-topped umbrella shape (umbel) typical of the carrot family. Multiple smaller umbels branch from the central stem to form a compound umbel. The plant is now 60–100cm tall. Hoverflies, bees, and beetles visit constantly on sunny days. If you crush a leaf it should smell faintly green but pleasant — never musty or unpleasant.

confidence_note: The drooping yellow flower clusters with orange/red spots inside are distinctive. Could be confused with Primrose, but Primrose flowers face upwards and are paler yellow.
summary: Golden yellow drooping flower clusters on chalk grassland — an indicator of ancient, undisturbed meadows. The orange spots inside each flower are diagnostic.
full_description:
Cowslips (Primula veris) are charming low-growing plants of chalk and limestone grasslands, old meadows, and field edges. Reaching only 10–25cm tall, they emerge in early spring as a rosette of wrinkled, oblong leaves before sending up flowering stems in April. The golden yellow flowers droop in characteristic one-sided clusters — each bell-shaped bloom has five notched petals and, crucially, orange or red spots at the petal base. Those spots are the best diagnostic feature, distinguishing Cowslips instantly from the similar Primrose. A sweet, light fragrance hangs over good patches on warm spring afternoons.

Cowslips are a reliable indicator of ancient, undisturbed chalk grassland. They cannot survive fields that have been ploughed or heavily fertilised, so large populations — like those at Old Down — tell you the grassland has been relatively undisturbed for many decades. At Old Down, Cowslips appear in April as one of the first great wildflower events of spring, sometimes carpeting entire slopes in golden yellow before most other flowers have opened.

The relationship between Cowslips and the Duke of Burgundy butterfly is one of nature's most specific partnerships: caterpillars feed almost exclusively on Cowslip and Primrose leaves, making good Cowslip populations essential for this nationally scarce butterfly, historically recorded at Old Down. The long-tongued Bombus hortorum (Garden Bumblebee) can reach nectar deep in the narrow flower tube that shorter-tongued insects cannot access, giving it a private food source in early spring.
native_info: Native throughout England and Wales, preferring chalky or limestone soils. Scarce in Scotland and north England. Common at Old Down and similar chalk grassland sites.
wildlife_value: A critical early nectar source for insects emerging from winter dormancy. Visited by early bumblebees, honeybees, Orange-tip butterflies, and hoverflies. The Garden Bumblebee (Bombus hortorum) has a tongue long enough to reach nectar deep in the flower tube. The leaves are the sole larval food plant for the Duke of Burgundy butterfly, a nationally scarce species historically recorded at Old Down.

life_stages.description: Cowslips emerge from winter dormancy as clusters of wrinkled, oval leaves lying flat against the ground in a rosette. Even at this stage, the distinctive leaf texture — wrinkled like crumpled paper, with a slightly rough surface — helps identify them from other early-spring plants. The leaves are 5–10cm long with a slightly irregular, wavy margin.

Flower stems begin to rise from the centre of the leaf rosette. The stems are slightly hairy and pale green. You can see the developing round buds forming in a cluster at the top of each stem. The buds are slightly darker yellow-green before they open.

Cowslips produce their iconic drooping clusters of golden yellow flowers. Look inside each flower — the orange or red spots at the petal base are diagnostic of this species. The nodding flower heads give the plant a distinctive bowing character quite unlike the upward-facing Primrose. At this peak stage, a single patch can contain dozens of flowering plants, creating a haze of golden yellow across the grassland. Each plant can have 2–5 flower stems.

confidence_note: Very small and fast-flying, easy to miss. Size (14–18mm wingspan) is the best first clue — smaller than any other blue butterfly you are likely to encounter.
summary: Britain's smallest butterfly — barely larger than a thumbnail. Males are bright silvery-blue; females brownish. Found only where Bird's-foot Trefoil grows on chalk or limestone grassland.
full_description: The Small Blue (Cupido minimus) is Britain's smallest butterfly, with a wingspan of just 14–18mm — about the size of a large fingernail. Despite its name, males are silvery-blue rather than vivid blue, and females are predominantly brown with just a dusting of blue at the wing base. Both sexes have pale grey-white undersides with small but neat black spots. They fly in a single generation each year (May–July), with a brief peak in June. Small Blues fly low and fast over short chalk grassland, making them easy to overlook unless you specifically search the knee-high vegetation. The species has an absolute dependence on its sole larval food plant, Bird's-foot Trefoil (Lotus corniculatus), and will only breed where this plant is present in sufficient quantity on well-drained, short-sward grassland. This makes the Small Blue an excellent indicator of chalk grassland health — its presence confirms a botanically rich, traditionally managed site.
native_info: Native to the UK. Found mainly in southern England and Wales on chalk and limestone grasslands. Colonies are typically small and localised. Old Down is excellent habitat.
wildlife_value: Adults feed on the nectar of Bird's-foot Trefoil, clovers, and vetches. Caterpillars have a fascinating relationship with ants (myrmecophily) — they secrete a sweet honeydew from a special gland, which ants feed on, in return protecting the caterpillar from predators. Their presence is a reliable indicator of high-quality chalk grassland.

life_stages.description: Female Small Blues lay tiny white eggs singly on the flower buds of Bird's-foot Trefoil (Lotus corniculatus). The eggs are so small they are almost impossible to spot without a magnifying glass. Each female may lay 30–60 eggs across her short adult life. Eggs hatch within about a week.

Caterpillars are tiny, green, and slug-like — quite different from the butterfly they will become. They feed on the flowers and developing seed pods of Bird's-foot Trefoil. From early in their development, caterpillars attract ants by secreting a sweet liquid from a special gland on their back. The ants tend them carefully, protecting them from parasitic wasps and other predators in exchange for this sugary reward.

life_stages.description: The caterpillar pupates on or near the Bird's-foot Trefoil plant, forming a small brown chrysalis that is exquisitely camouflaged against dead vegetation. This is the overwintering stage — the chrysalis remains dormant through autumn, winter, and into the following spring before the adult emerges in May or June of the following year.

Adults emerge in late May to early June and can be seen fluttering low over chalk grassland. Males are the first to emerge and can be seen patrolling their small territories. Females are slightly smaller and browner, spending more time at ground level searching for egg-laying sites on Bird's-foot Trefoil. Adults are short-lived — typically 2–3 weeks — but during warm weather can be seen in good numbers. At rest on a grass stem, the silvery underside with neat black spots is most visible.

confidence_note: Unmistakable. The stinging hairs on square stems and heart-shaped leaves are unique. You will know if you have misidentified it.
summary: The humble nettle is arguably the most ecologically important 'weed' in Britain. Caterpillar food plant for over 40 butterfly and moth species including Red Admiral, Peacock, and Small Tortoiseshell.
full_description: The Stinging Nettle (Urtica dioica) is the plant most people have an instinctive relationship with — usually an uncomfortable one. Growing 30–120cm tall with distinctive square stems, it forms dense clonal patches via underground rhizomes in hedgerows, field margins, woodland edges, and disturbed ground. The heart-shaped, deeply serrated leaves grow in opposite pairs. The entire plant — stems, leaves, and even the veins — is covered in hollow stinging hairs (trichomes) that inject a mixture of formic acid, histamine, and serotonin when touched, causing burning irritation that typically lasts 5–30 minutes. Dock leaves (Rumex obtusifolius), which commonly grow nearby, provide alkaline relief. Nettles are dioecious — male and female flowers grow on separate plants. Male flowers hang in long, drooping catkin-like clusters; female flowers are shorter and more upright. Its ecological importance is extraordinary: over 40 species of butterfly and moth caterpillar depend on it, including some of our most beloved garden butterflies.
danger_note: Stinging hairs cause temporary skin irritation lasting 5–30 minutes. Applying dock leaves (Rumex obtusifolius), which often grow nearby, provides relief. Not toxic — irritation only.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. One of the most common plants in Britain, found wherever there is nutrient-rich disturbed soil. An indicator of high-nitrogen soils.
wildlife_value: One of the most important plants in Britain for invertebrates. Over 40 butterfly and moth species use it as their caterpillar food plant, including Red Admiral, Peacock, Small Tortoiseshell, and Comma. Dense nettle patches provide shelter for beneficial insects, spiders, and small mammals. Finches eat the seeds in late summer. The plant's ecological value far outweighs the inconvenience of the sting. The seeds are nutritionally dense and considered adaptogenic — traditionally used as a tonic food, rich in fatty acids, protein, and minerals.

life_stages.description: In spring, Nettles emerge with fresh bright green shoots. Young plants have the same heart-shaped, serrated leaves as the adult but smaller and more tender. At this stage they are 10–30cm tall. Spring nettle tips were traditionally harvested for nettle soup — they are edible after thorough cooking destroys the sting. Still prickly though.

By late spring, nettle plants are 30–60cm tall with dense, lush foliage. Each square stem is clothed in opposite pairs of large, serrated leaves. At this stage the stinging hairs are fully developed — the lesson of not touching nettles becomes clear to young naturalists quickly.

life_stages.description: Nettles flower in summer and are wind-pollinated — they produce no nectar or showy petals. Male plants have long drooping clusters of small greenish flowers (catkins). Female plants have shorter, upright, more tightly clustered flowers. After pollination, female plants produce tiny seeds. During the flowering period, the plant is at its tallest, sometimes reaching 1.2m.

Dense stands turn yellow-brown in autumn. The dead stems remain standing through winter and provide hollow stem habitat for overwintering insects.

confidence_note: Sharp thorns, deeply lobed leaves, and either white flower clusters or red berries make this unmistakable in most seasons.
summary: The backbone of the British hedgerow. White blossom in May, red haws in autumn. Supports over 300 invertebrate species and feeds dozens of bird species — one of the most ecologically vital trees in Britain.
full_description: Hawthorn (Crataegus monogyna) is possibly the most ecologically important tree or shrub in the British landscape. A thorny deciduous shrub or small tree reaching 6–15m, it dominates most traditional British hedgerows. The deeply lobed leaves (3–5 lobes, resembling small oak leaves) emerge early in spring, giving the plant its country name 'May' from its spectacular white flowering in April–May. The sweetly fragrant flowers attract enormous numbers of pollinators — bees, hoverflies, beetles, and butterflies. By September, the hedgerow blazes red with ripe haws: small apple-like berries packed with energy for migrating and resident birds. The sharp thorns (5–15mm, modified shoot tips) create impenetrable cover for nesting birds and sheltering small mammals. Hawthorn supports over 300 species of invertebrate and provides food for dozens of bird species including Fieldfare, Redwing, and Waxwing. Its role in the British countryside — ecologically, historically, and culturally — is irreplaceable.
danger_note: Sharp thorns can cause skin punctures. Take care when working near hawthorn hedges.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. The dominant hedgerow shrub in Britain and one of the most abundant native trees. An indicator of ancient hedgerows when found in combination with other shrub species.
wildlife_value: One of the most important plants in Britain for wildlife. Supports over 300 invertebrate species as caterpillar food plant or shelter. The dense thorny growth is the most sought-after nesting and roosting site for many hedgerow birds. Berries (haws) provide critical autumn and winter food for Fieldfare, Redwing, Waxwing, Robin, Blackbird, and many other birds. Flowering provides essential early-season pollen and nectar.

life_stages.description: In winter, Hawthorn stands as a thorny tangle of dark grey-brown branches. The sharp thorns are fully visible and act as an important reminder of the plant's identity even when leafless. Small growth buds at the twig tips are already formed, swelling slowly. The dense growth provides critical roosting shelter for birds in cold weather.

Hawthorn is one of the first hedgerow shrubs to come into leaf in spring — often showing green by late February in mild years. The fresh, pale green leaves have a distinctive deeply lobed shape (3–5 lobes) that gives the plant a lacy appearance. The thorns become more obscured as foliage thickens. This bursting of green is what gave Hawthorn its country name 'May', celebrated in Mayday traditions.

life_stages.description: Hawthorn flowers create white clouds along hedgerows in late April and May. The clusters of small five-petalled white flowers are sweetly fragrant and provide essential nectar and pollen for an enormous range of insects. Flowers are sometimes faintly pink-tinged. The hawthorn's flowering is one of the great spectacles of the British spring.

life_stages.description: After flowering, the petals fall and tiny green berries (haws) begin to form. They remain hard and green through the summer months, gradually swelling. At this stage they are very astringent and inedible. The deep green foliage provides dense shade and nesting cover during the breeding season.

life_stages.description: The haws ripen through August and September, turning from green to orange to deep red. They soften and develop a slightly sweet, mealy flesh around a hard stone. Birds begin visiting in earnest as soon as the berries ripen. A well-berried hawthorn in September is one of the most productive wildlife habitats in the British countryside.

A large hawthorn may carry thousands of berries, providing critical fuel for migrating birds arriving from Scandinavia in October and November.

confidence_note: The deeply forked chestnut-red tail is unique among British raptors. Once seen, a Red Kite is unmistakable.
summary: One of Britain's greatest conservation success stories — nearly extinct by the 1980s, now soaring over southern England. The deeply forked chestnut tail is unmistakable.
full_description: The Red Kite (Milvus milvus) is one of Britain's most dramatic conservation successes. Nearly hunted to extinction by the early 20th century, with only a tiny relict population surviving in Wales, it was reintroduced to the Chilterns in 1989 and has since spread across much of England, Scotland, and Wales. A large, graceful raptor with a wingspan of 175–195cm, the Red Kite is unmistakable: warm russet-red plumage contrasts with a paler whitish-grey head, dark wingtips, pale patches on the underwings, and — most distinctively — a deeply forked, chestnut-red tail that is constantly twisted and angled in flight for manoeuvrability. It soars on thermals with effortless elegance, quite unlike the heavier-flapping Common Buzzard. Red Kites are opportunistic feeders, taking live prey including rabbits, hares, small mammals, and birds, but also readily eating carrion such as roadkill — a role that earns them the status of nature's waste disposal service. Their haunting mewing call can often be heard before the bird is seen.
native_info: Native to the UK. Reintroduction programme began in the Chilterns in 1989 and Scotland/Wales in the early 1990s. Now a resident breeding bird across much of southern and central England, spreading northward naturally.
wildlife_value: As a top predator and scavenger, Red Kites play an important role in the ecosystem by removing carrion and controlling populations of rabbits, voles, and other small animals. Their recovery is an indicator of improving raptor conservation and reduced persecution. Their presence is culturally significant — a powerful symbol of wildlife recovery.

life_stages.description: When perched, Red Kites show their full plumage clearly: russet-red body, streaked paler breast, whitish-grey head with dark streaks, and yellow bill and legs. The eyes are pale yellow. Their large size is apparent when perched on a fence post or telegraph pole. At rest, the forked tail is less obvious but the warm reddish-brown plumage is distinctive.

life_stages.description: In flight, the deeply forked chestnut-red tail is the most obvious identification feature — no other common British raptor has a forked tail. Red Kites are elegant soarers, using thermals to gain height while scanning below for food. The long, angled wings show pale patches on the undersides near the wingtips. The tail is constantly twisted and flexed to adjust direction, giving the bird a strikingly fluid quality in the air.

life_stages.description: Red Kites build large stick nests (eyries) in the forks of tall trees, adding new material each year until the nest becomes massive. They often incorporate odd human-made materials — plastic bags, scraps of clothing — into the nest lining, a quirk noted since medieval times. The female incubates 1–3 eggs for about 31–32 days. Adults can be seen making regular long-range hunting flights from the nest throughout the breeding season.

confidence_note: Unmistakable — hooked thorns, compound leaves, and either white-pink flowers or red/black berries at different times of year.
weather_note: Climate change is causing earlier fruiting by 2–3 weeks compared to historical norms. In warm springs, you may find ripe black berries from late July rather than the traditional August. Berries tend to be sweeter in warm autumns.
summary: Flowers in May–June, berries August–October. One of the most ecologically important plants in Britain — feeds over 100 insect species and dozens of bird and mammal species. Also yields the finest free food the British countryside has to offer.
full_description: Bramble, or Blackberry (Rubus fruticosus agg.), is a collective name covering hundreds of closely related microspecies within a complex aggregate. A scrambling, arching shrub growing 1–2m tall, it sprawls through hedgerows and scrub on long canes covered in hooked, backward-curving thorns that catch clothing and skin. The compound leaves usually have 3 (sometimes 5) oval, toothed leaflets. Bramble is effectively evergreen in mild winters, retaining some leaves year-round. In May–June, clusters of five-petalled white or pale pink flowers appear, intensely visited by pollinators. The familiar blackberries follow: each is a compound fruit made up of many small drupelets. Starting green and hard in July, they turn red, then ripen to glossy black in August–October. Bramble is ecologically one of the most important plants in Britain: flowers feed over 100 insect species, berries sustain birds and mammals through autumn, dense thorny growth shelters nesting birds, and leaves feed dozens of moth caterpillar species.
danger_note: Hooked thorns can cause scratches and snagging. Take care when picking berries in dense stands.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. One of the most common plants in Britain, found in virtually every hedgerow, woodland edge, and scrubby area.
wildlife_value: Flowers visited by over 100 insect species including bees, butterflies, hoverflies, and beetles. Berries eaten by Blackbird, Robin, Song Thrush, Waxwing, Wood Mouse, Fox, Badger, and Hedgehog. Dense thorny canes provide nesting sites for Whitethroat, Blackbird, and Wren. Many moth species use Bramble leaves as caterpillar food.

life_stages.description: In winter, Bramble stands as a tangle of woody arching canes with hooked thorns visible along their length. Some leaves remain (Bramble is semi-evergreen), often tinged red or purple in cold weather. The bare canes show the plant's structure clearly — long, arching stems that root where their tips touch the ground, gradually spreading the clump outward.

New bright green shoots emerge from the base of the plant and from existing canes. The fresh compound leaves are lighter green than the older leaves. Flower buds begin forming at the tips of the new growth. The plant expands rapidly in spring, new canes sometimes growing several centimetres per day in warm weather.

Bramble flowers from May to July (sometimes later), producing clusters of five-petalled flowers in white or pale pink. Each flower is 2–3cm across and sweetly scented. The extended flowering period — sometimes lasting 8–10 weeks — makes Bramble one of the most valuable nectar sources of the British summer. Bumblebees, honeybees, and many butterfly species visit constantly on warm days.

photos.caption: Bramble flowers — white five-petalled blossoms in clusters, UK
Bramble flowers close-up showing the five petals and stamens

life_stages.description: As flowers fade, berries begin to form. Initially the small drupelets are green and hard, gradually swelling. They then turn red — at which point they are very sour and astringent. On the same cane you may find both open flowers and berries at different stages of development, as Bramble flowers over such a long period.

photos.caption: Bramble with developing berries — green turning red

life_stages.description: Through August, the berries ripen from red to deep glossy black. When fully black and slightly soft to the touch, they are sweet and ready to eat. A natural sugar spike makes ripe brambles excellent forage for wildlife — and people. The Bramble picking season typically runs from mid-August to late September, though this is shifting earlier due to climate change.

photos.caption: Bramble berries ripening — mix of red and black on the same cane
Ripe blackberries — glossy black and ready to pick

life_stages.description: By September the berries are at their peak — deep black, soft, and sweet, with the best flavour after a warm summer. This is prime season for picking. Wildlife competition is intense: Blackbirds, Robins, Fieldfares, Waxwings, Wood Mice, Foxes, Badgers, and Hedgehogs all feed heavily on ripe brambles. By late October the remaining berries over-ripen and shrivel.

photos.caption: Fully ripe blackberries — peak picking season

similar_species.key_difference: Wild Raspberry has much finer, less hooked thorns, thinner and more delicate stems, and produces red (not black) berries. The berries are also hollow when picked (they come off the central plug), unlike Bramble berries which are solid.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Raspberry fruits earlier, mainly July–August

confidence_note: Count the spots: exactly 7 black spots on scarlet-red wing cases is diagnostic. 3 on each side plus 1 shared spot at the midline.
summary: Britain's most familiar beetle. Exactly 7 black spots on bright scarlet wing cases. A single adult eats 50–60 aphids per day — one of the most important natural pest controllers in Britain.
full_description: The 7-Spot Ladybird (Coccinella septempunctata) is Britain's most familiar beetle and one of the most recognisable insects in the world. At 7–8mm long, it has hemispherical, bright scarlet-red wing cases (elytra) bearing exactly seven black spots: three on each wing case plus one shared spot at the midline between them. The pronotum (the plate behind the head) is black with two small white spots at the front corners. The bright warning colouration (aposematism) deters predators — when threatened, ladybirds can secrete a bitter, toxic yellow fluid from leg joints (reflex bleeding) that is highly effective at deterring birds. They are among the most important natural pest controllers in Britain: a single adult can eat 50–60 aphids per day, and the larvae — which look completely unlike the adult, being spiky and black with yellow or orange spots — are even more voracious, consuming 100–150 aphids over their development. One of the gardener's and farmer's greatest allies.
native_info: Native to the UK and common throughout Britain. Populations can be temporarily displaced by the invasive Harlequin Ladybird in some areas, but the 7-Spot remains widespread.
wildlife_value: An essential natural pest controller. Reduces aphid populations without chemical intervention. Presence in a garden or field indicates a healthy, pesticide-free environment. Adults and larvae are also food for insectivorous birds, spiders, and ground beetles, making them part of the wider food chain.

life_stages.description: In autumn, 7-Spot Ladybirds seek sheltered sites for winter dormancy — under bark, in dense leaf litter, in hollow stems, or in crevices in walls. They often congregate in groups of dozens or more. They remain dormant through cold weather, relying on fat reserves built up during autumn feeding. On warm late-autumn or early-spring days they may briefly emerge before returning to shelter.

Active adults emerge from hibernation in March or April as temperatures rise. They feed on aphids, pollen, and nectar before mating in April–May. Adults are strong fliers and may travel considerable distances between aphid colonies. The distinctive scarlet and black pattern serves as a warning to predators that they are toxic and unpalatable. A freshly emerged adult after hibernation is as bright as ever — the colours do not fade with age.

photos.caption: 7-Spot Ladybird — the classic view showing all 7 black spots on scarlet wing cases
7-Spot Ladybird on vegetation
7-Spot Ladybird — spot pattern clearly visible
7-Spot Ladybird on plant, April

life_stages.description: Females lay clusters of 10–50 upright, yellow, oval eggs on plants where aphids are abundant — the hatching larvae will immediately have a food source. A female can lay up to 400 eggs over her lifetime, though many are eaten by other insects before hatching. Eggs hatch within 5–8 days depending on temperature.

Ladybird larvae look completely different from the adults and are often not recognised for what they are. They are elongated, dark grey or black, with bright yellow or orange spots, and carry small spiky projections along their backs. They are extremely mobile, walking long distances across plants in search of aphids. A single larva can eat 100–150 aphids during its 3–4 week development, making them even more valuable pest controllers than the adults.

photos.caption: 7-Spot Ladybird larva — black with yellow spots, very different from the adult
Ladybird larva on leaf showing the spiky, spotted appearance
Newly hatched 7-Spot Ladybird larva

life_stages.description: The larva attaches itself to a leaf or stem and pupates, forming a yellow-orange pupal case. The pupa is stationary and non-feeding — inside, the larva undergoes complete metamorphosis (holometabolism) into the adult form. The pupal stage lasts about 1–2 weeks. The adult that emerges is initially pale yellow, hardening and developing its full red colour within a few hours.

photos.caption: 7-Spot Ladybird pupa on a plant stem

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are native ladybird species on British plants
similar_species.key_difference: The 2-Spot Ladybird has only 2 black spots (one per wing case). It is also slightly smaller (4–6mm) and more variable in colour — some forms are black with red spots. Count the spots: 2 vs 7 makes identification straightforward.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both active March–October

similar_species.similarity_note: An invasive species now common in Britain
similar_species.key_difference: Harlequin Ladybird is larger (6–9mm), more domed, and extremely variable — it can have 0–22 spots in different colour combinations (red, orange, black). The most common form has many small spots. If a 'ladybird' looks unusually large or has an unusual spot pattern, it may be a Harlequin.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Harlequin is active March–October, as is 7-Spot

confidence_note: Smooth moist skin, dark mask through the eye, long back legs for jumping. Distinguished from Common Toad by smooth skin (toad is warty) and jumping rather than walking.
summary: Britain's most familiar amphibian. The life cycle — from jelly spawn to tadpole to froglet to adult — is one of nature's most dramatic transformations and an iconic sign of spring.
full_description: The Common Frog (Rana temporaria) is Britain's most widespread amphibian and one of the most beloved signs of spring. Adults are 5–9cm long with highly variable colouring — typically brown, olive, or grey with darker mottling, though reddish and yellowish forms also occur. The dark 'mask' running from the nostril through the eye to the shoulder, prominent golden-yellow eyes with horizontal slit pupils, and smooth but moist skin help distinguish frogs from the similar Common Toad. Frogs have powerful hind legs for jumping (50cm+ in a single leap) and are generally slimmer than toads. Their lifecycle is one of the most dramatic in nature: from jelly clumps of spawn in February–March, through free-swimming, algae-grazing tadpoles, to froglets emerging from the pond in June–July, to fully terrestrial adults that must nonetheless stay near water to keep their permeable skin moist. Adults return faithfully to their natal pond each spring, sometimes travelling hundreds of metres across roads and fields to breed.
native_info: Native throughout the UK and Ireland. One of the most common and widespread amphibians in Britain. Numbers have declined locally due to pond loss, drought, and disease (Ranavirus), but the species remains common.
wildlife_value: Tadpoles feed on algae (helping control algal blooms) and are food for newts, dragonfly larvae, diving beetles, and fish. Adults are important predators of slugs, snails, insects, and earthworms — of significant benefit in gardens and farms. Adults are themselves prey for herons, egrets, grass snakes, otters, and pike. A healthy frog population indicates a clean freshwater ecosystem.

life_stages.description: Frog spawn is laid in large gelatinous clumps in shallow, still water — ponds, ditches, or even large puddles and bird baths. Each clump can contain 1,000–3,000 black eggs, each surrounded by clear jelly that swells in water. The jelly protects the eggs and acts as a lens to warm them in weak spring sunlight. Multiple females often spawn in the same pond, creating vast aggregations. Spawn laid in too-shallow water or exposed to frost can be killed. The eggs hatch in 2–4 weeks, depending on temperature.

photos.caption: Common Frog spawn — black eggs in clear jelly clumps
Frogspawn in pond — a classic early spring sight
Frog spawn close-up showing individual eggs in jelly

life_stages.description: Tadpoles hatch as tiny, dark grey or black creatures with a large rounded head and a long, flattened tail for swimming. They breathe through feathery external gills at first, then internal gills as they develop. Tadpoles are primarily herbivores, grazing on algae using a specialised rasping mouth. They grow over 8–12 weeks from tiny hatchlings to fully formed tadpoles up to 3–4cm long. They are highly vulnerable to predation — newts, dragonfly larvae, diving beetles, and fish take enormous numbers.

photos.caption: Common Frog tadpoles feeding — dark bodies with long tails
Tadpoles in pond, feeding on algae
Frog tadpoles grazing

life_stages.description: After 8–12 weeks, the tadpole begins metamorphosis. Hind legs appear first, then front legs. The tail is gradually reabsorbed as the animal's digestive system switches from algae-grazing to insect-hunting. For a brief period the froglet has both legs and a tail — an extraordinary intermediate stage. Tiny froglets (just 1–2cm long) emerge from the pond in large numbers in June–July, often during or after rain, spreading into surrounding grassland and hedgerows. They must keep their skin moist and find shelter quickly.

photos.caption: Froglet at the final larval stage — legs developed, tail being reabsorbed

life_stages.description: Adult frogs live primarily on land in damp habitats — meadows, gardens, woodland floors — but must stay near water to keep their permeable skin moist. They breathe through both lungs and their moist skin. Adults hunt by sight, catching slugs, snails, worms, flies, and other small invertebrates with a rapid tongue strike. In autumn they seek damp, sheltered spots to hibernate through winter — under log piles, in compost heaps, or in pond mud. They emerge again in late winter (sometimes February in mild years) and make their way back to the breeding pond to spawn.

photos.caption: Common Frog adult — showing the dark eye mask and moist skin
Common Frog in profile showing typical brown colouring
Adult Common Frog — the colour pattern is highly variable
Adult Common Frog in grassland habitat

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are widespread British amphibians often found in the same habitats
similar_species.key_difference: Common Toad has warty, dry-looking skin (not smooth and moist). It is stockier, walks rather than hops, and has copper-coloured eyes (not golden). Toads are also generally larger (7–15cm vs 5–9cm for frogs).
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both spawn in spring, but Toads breed slightly later than Frogs (March–April vs February–March)

similar_species.similarity_note: A rarer British amphibian with similar colouring
similar_species.key_difference: Natterjack Toad has a distinctive yellow stripe running down the centre of its back — diagnostic and unmistakable. Also much rarer, mainly confined to sandy coasts and heathland. Extremely loud call.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Natterjack breeds later in spring than Common Frog

confidence_note: The song flight is unmistakable — a tiny bird hovering hundreds of feet up, singing continuously. On the ground it can look like a plain brown bird, but the small crest and streaky plumage are distinctive.
summary: Famous for its spectacular song flight — males rise vertically to 100m+ and sing continuously for minutes on end. A declining farmland bird, but still heard and seen on chalk grassland like Old Down.
full_description: The Skylark (Alauda arvensis) is one of the most celebrated birds of the British countryside, famed above all else for the extraordinary song flight of the male. A medium-sized songbird (16–18cm), it has streaky brown and buff plumage on the upperparts — the typical camouflage of a ground-nesting bird — with paler, streaked underparts, a small but distinctive crest on the crown (raised when singing or alarmed), and white outer tail feathers visible in flight. The Skylark is most often identified by sound: from March to August, males rise from the ground, ascending vertically to 50–100m or more, and deliver a continuous, complex, liquid warbling song lasting minutes or even hours without pause. This song flight — one of the finest sounds in British nature — serves to defend territory and attract mates. Unfortunately, the Skylark is in serious decline in the UK, having lost over 50% of its population since the 1970s due to intensification of arable farming, loss of wildflower meadows, and removal of the weed-rich field margins that young birds depend on for insect food.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. Partially migratory — some birds remain in the UK year-round; others migrate south to southern Europe and North Africa for winter. Populations at sites like Old Down are year-round residents on chalk grassland.
wildlife_value: Adult Skylarks eat seeds (particularly weed seeds) and insects. Chicks are fed almost exclusively on insects, grasshoppers, beetles, and invertebrate larvae from dense herbage — making insect-rich grassland and field margins essential for breeding success. Skylarks are themselves food for Sparrowhawk, Hobby, Peregrine, and occasionally Merlin in winter. Their presence on chalk grassland indicates a healthy, botanically rich ecosystem.

life_stages.description: In winter, Skylarks are quiet and inconspicuous. They gather in loose, shifting flocks of 10–50 birds on open farmland, grassland, or arable fields, foraging for seeds on the ground. In hard weather or cold spells, birds may move in larger flocks. The crest is often flattened at this time. Without the song to draw attention, winter Skylarks can easily be overlooked.

As days lengthen, male Skylarks establish territories on open grassland. The first tentative song flights begin in March — shorter and lower than the full summer performance, but unmistakably Skylark. Males begin competing for the best territories. Early spring is a good time to watch them at close range as they walk and run across the grassland with their characteristic upright posture.

photos.caption: Skylark on the ground in grassland, Lake District, UK — note the small crest

life_stages.description: From April to June, male Skylarks perform their most famous behaviour: spectacular song flights high above the grassland. Rising vertically while singing continuously, the male becomes a tiny speck against the sky at heights of 50–100m. The song is a rapid, bubbling, liquid warble — endlessly variable and extraordinarily sustained. A male may hold his position 100m up, singing, for 5–10 minutes or longer before parachuting back to earth. On still days at Old Down, a singing Skylark is one of the defining sounds of the site.

photos.caption: Skylark — perched male showing streaky plumage and raised crest
Skylark male, showing the characteristic upright stance

life_stages.description: Skylark nests are simple cups of grass, woven into a hollow scraped in the ground — usually well concealed in a grass tussock or clump of vegetation. The female incubates 3–4 speckled eggs for 11 days. Nests are highly vulnerable to agricultural operations (mowing, rolling) and predation from foxes, crows, and stoats. Successful pairs may raise 2–3 broods in a season.

Young Skylarks fledge at just 9–10 days old — before they can fly well — and are then fed on the ground for a further 2–3 weeks by both parents. During this period, the chicks are entirely dependent on insects: grasshoppers, beetles, flies, and caterpillars from dense grassland vegetation. The availability of insect-rich grassland margins is absolutely critical for chick survival — their loss to intensive farming is the primary cause of the Skylark's decline.

By August, the breeding season is over. Family groups and then larger flocks form, moving across farmland and grassland foraging for seeds. Some birds begin to drift southward, and Scandinavian birds arrive to winter in Britain. Song flights become rare, though you may still hear brief bursts on warm September days.

photos.caption: Skylark in late-season grassland, UK

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are brown, crested ground-nesting birds of open habitats
similar_species.key_difference: Woodlark is smaller with a shorter tail and more rounded wings. It has a distinctive black-and-white stripe over the eye. Its song is also different — a beautiful liquid descending phrase, not the Skylark's sustained warble. Prefers woodland edges and heath rather than open grassland.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Woodlark is resident year-round but much less common in the UK

similar_species.similarity_note: Another small, streaky brown bird of grassland habitats
similar_species.key_difference: Meadow Pipit is smaller and slimmer, with a much finer bill. It has no crest. Its song flight is shorter and the call is a thin 'seep seep seep'. It bobs its tail frequently when walking, unlike Skylark.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Meadow Pipits are common year-round on chalk grassland alongside Skylarks

summary: Tall white daisies with golden yellow centres that stand above the summer grassland at Old Down in great drifts. One of Britain's most cheerful wildflowers — and a magnet for hoverflies, bees, and beetles.
full_description:
Oxeye Daisy (Leucanthemum vulgare) is one of the most recognisable wildflowers in Britain — the classic large daisy of summer meadows, with bright white ray petals surrounding a golden yellow disc. Plants grow 30–70cm tall, with slightly waxy toothed leaves that clasp the stem, and can form dense colonies in undisturbed grassland. Individual flowers are 3–5cm across, much larger than any other common white daisy, and held on long unbranched stems.

At Old Down, Oxeye Daisy produces spectacular displays across the chalk grassland from June through July. It thrives in the low-nutrient, well-drained chalk soil and is one of the easiest ways to spot ancient, unimproved meadow — it struggles where soil has been enriched with fertiliser. The flowers are open-structured and produce large amounts of pollen and nectar accessible to a wide range of insects, making patches of Oxeye Daisy some of the best places at Old Down to watch insects in summer.

Oxeye Daisy can be confused with similar-looking relatives like Scentless Mayweed, but is distinguished by its larger flowers, clasping stem-leaves, and taller growth. It is also noticeably scentless — crush the leaves and they have a faint, slightly aromatic smell, but nothing like the pineapple scent of Pineapple Mayweed.
native_info: Native throughout the UK in meadows, grasslands, roadsides, and disturbed ground, especially on well-drained and chalk soils. One of the most common meadow wildflowers where grassland is unimproved.
wildlife_value: One of the most visited flowers at Old Down in summer. The open disc provides abundant pollen and nectar accessible to hoverflies, solitary bees, bumblebees, beetles, and many butterfly species including Meadow Brown and Common Blue. Seed heads are eaten by finches in late summer.

life_stages.description: In spring, Oxeye Daisy grows as a flat rosette of deeply toothed, slightly waxy dark green leaves close to the ground. The leaves are spoon-shaped with rounded teeth. At this stage it can be confused with other rosette plants, but the leaf shape is distinctive.

Stems rise to 30–70cm and produce the large white-and-gold daisy flowers. At peak flowering in June–July, Old Down grassland can be dotted with hundreds of flowers simultaneously. Each flower head is 3–5cm across with 15–30 white ray florets surrounding the golden disc. Flowers close slightly in dull weather and fully at night.

photos.caption: Oxeye Daisy close-up showing white ray petals and golden disc
Oxeye Daisy in grassland habitat

life_stages.description: After flowering, the ray petals fall and the central disc forms a small seed head. Seeds are ribbed and cylindrical, dispersed by wind and animals. Plants die back in autumn but re-grow strongly the following spring.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both white-rayed daisies common in summer
similar_species.key_difference: Scentless Mayweed is smaller (1–2cm flowers), has very finely divided feathery leaves, and a hollow domed centre disc. Oxeye Daisy has larger flowers, solid stem, and clasping toothed leaves.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both flower June–September

photos.caption: Oxeye Daisy — classic white and gold summer flower
Oxeye Daisy in chalk grassland

summary: Deep purple thistle-like flowers that attract an extraordinary range of butterflies to Old Down in summer. Watch a patch of Knapweed on a warm July day and you might count six or seven butterfly species in an hour.
full_description:
Common Knapweed (Centaurea nigra) is one of the most ecologically valuable wildflowers of chalk grassland. Reaching 30–90cm tall, it has stiff branched stems, slightly rough oblong leaves, and produces tough, brush-like purple flower heads from July through September. The flower head has a distinctive blackish-brown papery base (the 'knap'), giving the plant its name. Flowers are deep reddish-purple, resembling a small thistle but with no spines on the leaves.

At Old Down, Common Knapweed is one of the signature plants of high summer. On warm days in July and August, single clumps can attract Marbled White, Meadow Brown, Common Blue, Small Skipper, and Gatekeeper butterflies simultaneously — along with dozens of bumblebees and hoverflies. The flowers produce abundant nectar accessible to many insects, and the ripe seed heads are important food for Goldfinches in late summer and autumn.

Common Knapweed is sometimes confused with Greater Knapweed (Centaurea scabiosa), which also grows at Old Down. Greater Knapweed has conspicuous outer florets that spread out in rays around the flower head — like a crown — and deeply divided, feathery leaves. Common Knapweed has a simpler, brush-like flower head with no ray florets, and less divided leaves.
native_info: Native and common throughout England and Wales in meadows, grasslands, and roadsides, especially on well-drained soils including chalk. One of the signature species of lowland meadow and chalk grassland habitats.
wildlife_value: One of the most important nectar plants at Old Down. Visited by Marbled White, Meadow Brown, Common Blue, Gatekeeper, and Small Skipper butterflies, as well as multiple bumblebee species and hoverflies. Seed heads are eaten by Goldfinch and other finches. Caterpillars of several moth species feed on the leaves and stems.

life_stages.description: Knapweed grows as clumps of rough, oblong leaves in spring. The leaves are slightly grey-green with a rough texture. Stems begin to elongate in May–June before flowering begins.

The classic reddish-purple flower heads open from July, each on a tough stiff stem. The blackish-brown bracts at the base of each flower head are diagnostic — squeeze one gently and feel the stiff papery scales. At peak flowering a single established plant can carry 10–20 flower heads simultaneously.

photos.caption: Common Knapweed flowers in chalk grassland
Common Knapweed close-up showing the distinctive blackish bracts

life_stages.description: After flowering, the heads become papery seed heads that Goldfinches prize highly in autumn. Each seed has a small tuft of bristles and is spread by wind. The dried stems persist through winter, providing structure in the landscape.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both Centaurea species growing in the same habitats at Old Down
similar_species.key_difference: Greater Knapweed (Centaurea scabiosa) has larger flowers with conspicuous spreading outer ray florets forming a fringe, and deeply divided, feathery leaves. Common Knapweed has a simpler brush-like flower head with no rays, and less divided leaves.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both flower July–September

photos.caption: Common Knapweed — one of Old Down's best butterfly nectar plants
Common Knapweed showing dark bracts at flower base

summary: Small but enormously important — this is the only food plant for Small Blue caterpillars. The bright yellow flowers tipped with orange-red give it the nickname 'Eggs and Bacon'. Grow on the chalk slopes and search carefully for the tiny black eggs laid on the flower buds.
full_description:
Bird's-foot Trefoil (Lotus corniculatus) is a low-growing member of the pea family, rarely reaching more than 30cm tall. It has small trefoil (three-leaflet) leaves with two additional leaflets at the leaf base — technically making it five-leafed. The bright yellow flowers are held in clusters of 2–7 and are streaked or tipped with orange-red, giving the plant its vivid nickname. When the seed pods ripen they spread in a claw-like pattern, like a bird's foot — the origin of the other common name.

At Old Down, Bird's-foot Trefoil is one of the most ecologically critical plants on the site. It is the sole larval food plant for the Small Blue butterfly — the only plant the caterpillars will eat — and also used by Common Blue caterpillars. Without good populations of Bird's-foot Trefoil on the chalk slopes, neither butterfly could survive here. It grows in low, well-drained turf and thrives where rabbit grazing keeps the grass short — which is one reason rabbits are so important to the ecology of Old Down.

The flowers are excellent for watching insects: bumblebees, particularly the long-tongued Garden Bumblebee, feed on the nectar, and several moth species use it as a caterpillar food plant. On warm summer days, Small Blue adults can often be found nectaring on the very plants their caterpillars depended on the previous year.
native_info: Native throughout the UK in short grassland, especially on well-drained and chalk soils. Common on roadsides, meadows, and coastal cliffs. Thrives in low-nutrient conditions.
wildlife_value: The sole larval food plant for Small Blue butterfly caterpillars — one of the most specific ecological relationships at Old Down. Also used by Common Blue caterpillars and the Six-spot Burnet moth. Excellent nectar source for bumblebees, especially long-tongued species. Fixes atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil quality for surrounding plants.

life_stages.description: Low spreading mats of trefoil leaves emerge in spring. The leaves are small, bright green, and slightly hairy. The plant grows close to the ground, spreading outward from a central taproot.

Clusters of 2–7 pea-like flowers appear from June through August. Each flower is yellow, often tipped or streaked with orange-red, held on a thin stem above the leaves. Look carefully at open flower buds — Small Blue butterflies lay their tiny eggs directly on the flower buds. The eggs are minute white spheres, visible with good eyes or a hand lens.

photos.caption: Bird's-foot Trefoil showing the classic yellow-and-orange flowers
Bird's-foot Trefoil flowers in chalk grassland

life_stages.description: After flowering, the seed pods develop as slender dark brown pods that spread in a claw or bird's-foot pattern. The pods pop open when ripe and can be heard cracking on hot dry days.

similar_species.similarity_note: A closely related species sometimes growing in the same area
similar_species.key_difference: Greater Bird's-foot Trefoil (Lotus pedunculatus) is taller, up to 60cm, with hollow stems and prefers damp grassland, marshes, and fens rather than dry chalk. Common Bird's-foot Trefoil has solid stems and grows in drier conditions.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both flower June–August

photos.caption: Bird's-foot Trefoil — critical food plant for Small Blue caterpillars
Bird's-foot Trefoil flowers in close-up

summary: The common grassland plant with dark, oval flower heads on tall wiry stems. It can survive heavy trampling because its tough, ribbed leaves grow flat to the ground. Look for the circle of creamy white stamens as the pollen is released.
full_description:
Ribwort Plantain (Plantago lanceolata) is one of the most abundant wildflowers in British grasslands — easy to overlook, but fascinating once you know it. The leaves form a flat rosette, each leaf narrow-oval with three to five prominent parallel ribs (veins) running along their length — the 'ribwort' of its name. The flower stems are long, slender, and deeply ridged, reaching 10–50cm, and are topped by a dark, oval-cylindrical spike.

The flowers themselves are tiny but beautiful at close range: as the spike matures, a ring of cream or pale yellow stamens emerges from the bottom of the spike and works its way upward, giving the head a halo-like appearance. The plant is wind-pollinated and releases clouds of pollen — important to know for hay fever sufferers. Seeds are enclosed in a papery capsule that splits to release two seeds.

Ribwort Plantain has been used in traditional medicine for centuries — the leaves were applied to wounds as a poultice and contain compounds that may have mild anti-inflammatory properties. The tough, flat rosette survives trampling better than most plants, which is why it appears along well-used paths and in lawns as well as in pristine meadows. At Old Down it grows throughout the chalk grassland and is an important caterpillar food plant for several moth species.
native_info: Native throughout the UK in almost all grassland, path-side, and disturbed habitats. One of the most widespread plants in temperate climates globally.
wildlife_value: Caterpillar food plant for the Heath Fritillary, Glanville Fritillary, and several moth species. Seeds are eaten by Goldfinch and other finches. Pollen is wind-dispersed and very abundant. The plant provides shelter and climbing structure for many small invertebrates in grassland.

life_stages.description: The distinctive flat rosette of narrow-ribbed leaves lies close to the ground. Each leaf has 3–5 prominent parallel veins — run your finger along the leaf and you can feel the ribs clearly. The leaves are tough and slightly hairy, which is why they survive being trodden on.

photos.caption: Ribwort Plantain rosette of ribbed leaves

life_stages.description: Long ridged flower stems rise from the rosette, each topped with a dark oval spike 1–4cm long. As each flower matures, a circle of pale cream stamens appears and moves up the spike — this gives the head a halo effect and is the easiest way to see that the plant is in flower. On still days you can see pollen dusting from the anthers.

photos.caption: Ribwort Plantain flower spike showing the ring of cream stamens

life_stages.description: The spike dries and turns brown. Small papery seed capsules each hold two seeds. Goldfinches and linnets pick at the dried heads through late summer and autumn.

similar_species.similarity_note: Another common plantain often growing in the same locations
similar_species.key_difference: Greater Plantain (Plantago major) has broad oval leaves and a long narrow cylindrical spike on a stout, un-ridged stem. Ribwort Plantain has narrow lance-shaped leaves and an oval stubby spike on a furrowed stem.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both flower May–October
