Ribwort Plantain flower spike with stamens

summary: One of Britain's most important wildflowers — not a weed. Golden flowers in early spring are a lifeline for queen bumblebees just waking from winter. The round white clock seed heads are irresistible to blow and each one carries seeds that can travel kilometres on the wind.
full_description:
The Dandelion (Taraxacum officinale agg.) is one of the most ecologically valuable and overlooked wildflowers in Britain. What looks like a single golden flower is actually a composite head of 100–200 tiny individual flowers, each containing both pollen and nectar. The deeply toothed leaves — 'dent de lion' (lion's tooth in French) is the origin of the name — grow in a flat rosette, with the teeth pointing back towards the centre. All parts produce a milky white latex sap when broken. Plants can grow 5–40cm tall.

In early spring, Dandelions are one of the first flowers to open after winter, often by February in mild weather. At this time they provide an absolutely critical food source for queen bumblebees that have recently emerged from hibernation and need energy before they can establish their new colonies. Without early-flowering plants like Dandelions, queen bumblebees may fail. They are also one of the first nectar sources for Orange-tip and Small Tortoiseshell butterflies. Dandelions continue flowering sporadically through summer and autumn, with a second peak in late summer.

The seed clock — a perfect sphere of parachuted seeds — is an engineering masterpiece. Each seed has a parachute of fine bristles (a pappus) that generates a vortex ring in the air, allowing seeds to stay aloft far longer than their weight would suggest. A single plant can produce 200 seeds per head, with several heads per plant. Goldfinches and other finches eat the seeds before they fully disperse. Note: Dandelion is technically an aggregate species — there are actually hundreds of micro-species within the Taraxacum group, distinguishable only by specialists.
native_info: Native throughout the UK in almost every habitat. Abundant in meadows, lawns, roadsides, and disturbed ground. One of the most widespread plants in the northern hemisphere.
wildlife_value: Critical early nectar and pollen source for queen bumblebees emerging from hibernation in February–March. Visited by over 100 species of insect including many specialist mining bees. Seeds eaten by Goldfinch, Linnet, and Greenfinch. Leaves eaten by many moth caterpillars and by rabbits. One of the most important plants for urban and rural wildlife alike.

life_stages.description: The deeply toothed, strap-shaped leaves form a flat rosette at ground level, present all year in mild conditions. The lobes of each leaf point backwards towards the base — run your finger from tip to base and feel them pointing back like the teeth of a lion (dent de lion). Snap a leaf and white milky latex sap oozes out.

photos.caption: Dandelion leaves showing the deeply toothed 'lion's tooth' lobes

life_stages.description: The hollow, leafless flower stems rise from the rosette, each topped with a single golden flower head made up of 100–200 individual ray florets. Flowers close at night and in dull weather. On sunny days they open fully and are covered in insects. The first flowers can appear as early as February in mild years.

photos.caption: Dandelion flower in full bloom

life_stages.description: After flowering, the golden head closes for a day or two before reopening as the perfect spherical seed clock — a globe of white parachuted seeds, each attached to a single seed by a stalk of fine bristles. The whole structure is 3–5cm across. On still days seeds drift slowly upward; on windy days they can travel hundreds of metres. Count the puffs it takes to blow all the seeds off — and check the time!

photos.caption: Dandelion clock — perfect sphere of parachuted seeds
Dandelion seed head close-up showing parachute bristles

similar_species.similarity_note: Both produce yellow dandelion-type flowers in grassland
similar_species.key_difference: Cat's-ear (Hypochaeris radicata) has branched flower stems (Dandelion stems are unbranched), solid stems (Dandelion stems are hollow), and smaller rougher leaves with rounder lobes. Cat's-ear also has small scale-like leaves on the stem.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both flower spring–autumn, Cat's-ear peaks June–September

photos.caption: Dandelion — one of Britain's most important early wildflowers
Dandelion clock — perfect sphere ready for dispersal
Dandelion seed parachutes close-up
Dandelion leaves — deeply toothed like a lion's teeth

weather_note: White blossom appears before the leaves and can open anywhere from late February in warm years to late April in cold springs. 'Blackthorn winter' is the cold spell that sometimes returns when Blackthorn is in bloom.
summary: The shrub that turns pure white before it even has leaves in spring — the blossom appears on black, bare spiny branches, creating one of the most dramatic sights in the early hedgerow. Then in autumn the same branches are covered in dark blue-black sloe berries.
full_description:
Blackthorn (Prunus spinosa) is a dense, thorny shrub or small tree that is one of the most important components of chalk grassland hedgerows and scrub. It can grow to 5m tall and spreads by suckers, forming impenetrable thickets. The branches are very dark, almost black, with stiff sharp spines — the 'blackthorn' of its name, contrasting with the white-barked Hawthorn. The leaves are small, oval, and finely toothed, appearing after the blossom.

The timing of Blackthorn blossom is one of the most dramatic events in the spring hedgerow. Before a single leaf has opened, the bare black branches become smothered in pure white 5-petalled flowers in March or April, creating a cloud of white visible from a distance. This cold, bright-blossomed period is often called a 'Blackthorn winter' because a cold spell frequently accompanies or follows the blossom. The timing varies significantly year to year — by several weeks — depending on spring temperatures.

In autumn, the transformation is equally dramatic: the blossom positions are replaced by sloe berries — dark blue-black, heavily bloomed (with a waxy powder coating), and very astringent if eaten raw. After the first frosts, the sloes soften and become less sharp, and are the basis of sloe gin. Thrushes, Fieldfares, and Redwings eat sloes enthusiastically in autumn. The dense, thorny thickets provide nesting sites for Yellowhammer, Whitethroat, and Linnet at Old Down.
danger_note: The thorns are sharp and can cause deep puncture wounds. Blackthorn thorns are known to cause infection if they break off under the skin. Handle with care when working near these shrubs.
native_info: Native throughout the UK in hedgerows, woodland edges, scrub, and chalk and limestone downland. One of the most important native shrubs for wildlife.
wildlife_value: Provides critical early pollen and nectar for queen bumblebees, mining bees, and early butterflies when few other plants are in flower. Sloe berries are a major food source for thrushes (Fieldfare, Redwing, Blackbird) in autumn and winter. Dense thorny thickets provide safe nesting for Yellowhammer, Whitethroat, and Linnet. Caterpillars of Brown Hairstreak butterfly feed exclusively on young Blackthorn shoots.

life_stages.description: In winter, Blackthorn is a stark dark shrub of nearly black bare spiny branches. The darkness of the stems is distinctive and gives the plant its name. The very dark stems contrast sharply with the grey-white bark of Hawthorn in the same hedgerow.

One of the most spectacular events in the early hedgerow — pure white 5-petalled flowers covering the bare black branches before a single leaf has appeared. Each flower is 1–1.5cm across with prominent yellow stamens. The blossom can appear as early as late February in warm years. This is the most reliable time to identify the plant with certainty.

photos.caption: Blackthorn in full blossom on bare branches — one of spring's most dramatic hedgerow sights
Blackthorn blossom close-up showing the characteristic pure white flowers

life_stages.description: After blossom, small oval, finely toothed leaves appear. The shrub is now green, denser and less distinctive. Look for the sharp spines — these are true spines (modified branches) and are very stiff and sharp. In summer, developing sloe berries can be seen as small hard green spheres.

The berries turn from green to dark blue-black and develop a waxy bloom (pale grey powder coating). Ripe sloes in October are beautiful — dark, round, and covered in this misty bloom. They are very astringent raw, but after the first frosts (or a night in the freezer) the flesh softens slightly. Thrushes, Fieldfares, and Redwings descend on ripe sloe bushes in October.

photos.caption: Ripe sloe berries with characteristic waxy bloom

similar_species.similarity_note: Both thorny shrubs growing in the same hedgerows at Old Down
similar_species.key_difference: Hawthorn flowers after its leaves appear (May), while Blackthorn flowers before any leaves (March–April). Hawthorn has grey-brown bark and red berries (haws). Blackthorn has very dark nearly black bark and blue-black berries (sloes).
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Blossom timing is the clearest separation: Blackthorn = March–April, bare branches; Hawthorn = May, with leaves

photos.caption: Blackthorn blossom on bare black branches — a sign of very early spring
Blackthorn blossom close-up
Ripe sloe berries with waxy blue-black bloom

summary: The hovering falcon — kestrels can hang motionless in the air while they use ultraviolet vision to track vole runs in the grass below. Old Down's open chalk grassland is perfect hunting ground. Watch the sky above the slope and you will nearly always spot one.
full_description:
The Kestrel (Falco tinnunculus) is Britain's most familiar bird of prey, and the one most likely to be seen hovering over roadside verges, motorway embankments, and open grasslands. Males have a striking blue-grey head and tail, chestnut-brown back with black spots, and a cream-buff breast with dark streaks. Females and juveniles are brown all over with barring on the back and tail. In flight, the long narrow pointed wings and long tail are distinctive; in a hover, the tail fans out and the wingtips vibrate rapidly while the head stays perfectly still — an extraordinary feat of aerodynamics.

Kestrels hunt primarily by hovering 10–30m above the ground, facing into the wind, with their eyesight focused on a remarkably small area of ground. They can detect ultraviolet light, which means they can see the urine trails left by voles — voles mark their runs with urine that reflects UV light strongly, effectively laying out a map of the best hunting spots. When prey is located, the kestrel drops in stages — hover, drop, hover again — before stooping rapidly to catch the prey in its talons.

At Old Down, Kestrels hunt the open chalk grassland and field margins throughout the year. Their main prey here is Field Voles, with occasional Shrews, large insects (especially in summer), and small birds. Breeding pairs nest in tree holes, cliff ledges, or old crow nests in trees around the site perimeter, with young fledging in June–July. Kestrel populations have declined significantly in lowland England since the 1970s, largely due to agricultural intensification reducing vole habitat — making chalk grassland sites like Old Down increasingly important.
native_info: Resident and widespread throughout the UK. Most common in open habitats including grassland, heathland, farmland, and motorway verges. Has declined by about 50% in lowland England since the 1970s.
wildlife_value: Controls Field Vole and Wood Mouse populations. Indicator species for open grassland habitat quality — a Kestrel hunting overhead means there is a healthy grassland invertebrate and small mammal community below. Also preys on large insects, helping regulate invertebrate populations.

life_stages.description: Blue-grey head and tail, chestnut-brown back with black teardrop spots, cream-buff underside with dark streaks. In flight from below, the tail is a clean blue-grey fan. This is the plumage most people associate with the Kestrel.

photos.caption: Male Kestrel showing blue-grey head and chestnut back

life_stages.description: The signature behaviour: head completely still while wings beat rapidly and tail fans open. The kestrel faces into the wind and maintains a fixed position in the air, scanning the ground below for movement. The head points downward at a slight angle. This behaviour is easier to see on windy days when less wing-flapping is needed.

photos.caption: Kestrel in classic hover — head perfectly still, wings and tail spread

life_stages.description: Young Kestrels leave the nest in June–July and look similar to adult females — brown with barring. They are often seen in late summer practising hovering, sometimes less smoothly than adults. The family group may remain loosely together for several weeks after fledging.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both common raptors at Old Down
similar_species.key_difference: Sparrowhawk has short rounded wings and a long tail — it flies fast through woodland and hedgerows in a series of rapid flaps and glides, never hovering. Kestrel has long pointed wings and hovers regularly. Sparrowhawk has barred underparts.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both present year-round

photos.caption: Kestrel hovering — the behaviour that makes it instantly identifiable
Male Kestrel perched, showing blue-grey head and chestnut back

summary: Britain's unofficial national bird and one of the most familiar — the orange-red breast is visible from a long way off. Robins are unusually confiding and will often follow people digging or clearing vegetation, waiting for disturbed worms and insects.
full_description:
The Robin (Erithacus rubecula) is one of Britain's most recognisable birds, with its warm orange-red breast, white belly, brown back, and large, expressive dark eyes. Both male and female have identical plumage — unusually for British birds. Adults are about 14cm long, rounded in shape, and tend to perch upright with a slight lean forward. The song is a rich, wistful, melodic warble, heard in every month of the year including winter, when Robins sing at night under streetlights.

Robins are famously territorial and will vigorously defend their patch against other Robins — a puffed-up chest display to show off the red breast is a threat display, and physical fights do occur. They are also unusually confiding around humans, having evolved alongside animals that disturb soil — historically wild boar, now gardeners and walkers. This is why a Robin will often appear when you dig the garden, perching nearby and darting in for earthworms and beetles.

At Old Down, Robins inhabit the hedgerows, scrub, and woodland edge around the site perimeter. They nest in low hedgerow, in crevices, or on the ground in dense vegetation, building a cup of dead leaves and moss. Young Robins look completely different to adults — they are brown and heavily spotted, with no red breast at all, which confuses many people who encounter them in summer.
native_info: Resident throughout the UK, one of the most abundant birds. Found in almost all habitats with some shrub or tree cover. Partially migratory — UK Robins are mostly resident but are joined by Continental Robins in winter.
wildlife_value: Insectivore, earthworm specialist, and berry-eater in autumn and winter. Controls populations of soil invertebrates. Nest sites and territorial patterns shape the spatial use of hedgerows and scrub at Old Down.

life_stages.description: The classic Robin — orange-red breast (the colour is technically orange, not red), brown back, large dark eyes, and white belly. Posture is upright with a slight forward lean. Often bobs up and down nervously. The song is a wistful, cascading warble, quite different from any other garden bird.

photos.caption: Robin showing the iconic orange-red breast
Robin with characteristic alert posture and head tilt

life_stages.description: Young Robins fledge in May–June and look completely different from adults. They are warm brown all over with pale buff spots on the breast and back — no orange-red at all. The spots are gradually replaced by adult plumage through a moult in late summer. Many people mistake juvenile Robins for a different species entirely.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both small, brown, ground-foraging birds that can appear similar at a glance
similar_species.key_difference: Dunnock is grey on the face and breast with brown streaked back, no orange breast at all. Dunnock creeps mouse-like along the ground; Robin stands more upright. The Dunnock's bill is finer and more pointed.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both present year-round

photos.caption: Robin — Britain's most beloved garden bird
Robin in characteristic alert pose

summary: The acrobatic jewel of the hedgerow — a Blue Tit can hang completely upside down from the thinnest twig while it picks off insects and larvae. The vivid blue-and-yellow combination makes it one of Britain's most colourful small birds.
full_description:
The Blue Tit (Cyanistes caeruleus) is one of Britain's most colourful and familiar small birds — bright blue cap, wings and tail, yellow breast, white cheeks with a dark eye stripe, and a thin dark line running down the yellow belly. Males are slightly brighter than females, but the difference is subtle. Blue Tits are tiny — just 12cm long and about 11 grams — but they are energetic and acrobatic, able to hang upside down on the thinnest twigs to access food.

Blue Tits are particularly important predators of caterpillars in spring. A breeding pair with a nest full of chicks can collect up to 1,000 caterpillars per day from the surrounding trees — and they time their breeding to coincide with the peak of caterpillar emergence from oak trees. If the spring is warm and caterpillars emerge early, but the tits start nesting on the traditional date, they may miss the peak. This timing mismatch, driven by climate change, is one of the most studied ecological problems in British birds.

At Old Down, Blue Tits are most visible in the hedgerows and scrub around the site perimeter. In autumn and winter they join roving mixed-species flocks with Great Tits, Long-tailed Tits, and Treecreepers, moving through the hedgerow together. The loud, scolding 'tsee-tsee-tsee' alarm call and the 'churring' contact notes are distinctive once learned.
native_info: Resident and abundant throughout England, Wales, and Scotland. Most common in woodland and woodland edge, but adapts well to gardens, hedgerows, and urban areas. One of Britain's most numerous birds.
wildlife_value: Major predator of caterpillars, aphids, and other small invertebrates. A single breeding pair may remove tens of thousands of invertebrates from an area during the breeding season. Nest holes used after abandonment by other species including some insects. Seeds of sunflowers and teasels eaten in winter.

life_stages.description: Vivid blue cap, wing-coverts and tail; bright yellow breast with a faint dark line down the centre; white cheeks with a dark eye stripe. The blue of the cap can appear almost electric on a sunny day. Both sexes are identical in general appearance, though males tend to be slightly brighter blue on the cap.

photos.caption: Blue Tit adult showing vivid blue cap and yellow breast

life_stages.description: Eggs are laid in April–May in a nest box or tree hole. Chicks hatch after two weeks and fledge at about three weeks. Juveniles have yellow-green on the face and breast (replacing the white cheeks) and duller blue. They are often seen in family groups in July, noisily following parents through hedgerows.

similar_species.similarity_note: Closely related, often in the same flocks
similar_species.key_difference: Great Tit is larger (14cm vs 12cm), has a bold black stripe running down a yellow breast, a black head with white cheeks, and no blue on the cap or wings. The Great Tit's song is the familiar 'tea-cher tea-cher' repeated call.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both present year-round

photos.caption: Blue Tit — one of Britain's most colourful small birds

summary: Britain's largest and most common pigeon — the clattering rush of wings as a flock launches from the treetops is an unmistakable countryside sound. Look for the distinctive white neck patches that flash in flight. The cooing call is one of the most soothing sounds of the British countryside.
full_description:
The Woodpigeon (Columba palumbus) is Britain's most abundant pigeon and one of the most numerous birds in the country, with a population of around 5.4 million breeding pairs. It is substantially larger than Feral Pigeon or Stock Dove — 41cm long with a wingspan of 75–80cm — blue-grey above, with a pinkish-grey breast, and the diagnostic white patches on each side of the neck (absent in young birds). In flight, the white crescents on each wing are very visible. The soft, repetitive cooing call — 'coo-COO-coo, coo-coo' — is one of the most characteristic sounds of British countryside and woodland edge.

Woodpigeons are almost entirely herbivorous, eating an enormous variety of plant material including grain, berries, seeds, leaves, and buds. They have a crop — a pouch in the throat — that allows them to carry large volumes of food back to their nest. Young Woodpigeons (squabs) are fed 'crop milk' — a protein-rich liquid produced by both parents from cells lining the crop — which is unusual among birds and means they can breed at almost any time of year when food is available.

At Old Down, Woodpigeons feed in the open grassland and field edges, and roost and nest in the hedgerows and scrub. They are an important prey item for Peregrine Falcon, which hunts over the site, and for Goshawk in nearby woodland. Large flocks gather on farmland near the site in autumn to feed on harvested fields.
native_info: Abundant resident throughout the UK. Found in almost all habitats with trees or hedgerows. Has increased significantly in population since the 1960s. One of Britain's most common birds.
wildlife_value: Major prey item for Peregrine Falcon, Goshawk, and Sparrowhawk. Seeds passed through the gut are dispersed widely. Nest sites used by other species. Provides a substantial food source for raptors — the presence of large Woodpigeon flocks near Old Down partly explains the regular Red Kite and occasional Peregrine sightings.

life_stages.description: Large, heavy-bodied pigeon with blue-grey plumage. The white neck patches are the most distinctive feature — white crescents on each side of the neck with iridescent green-purple plumage below them. The breast is pinkish-grey. In flight, white wing bars flash across each wing. Eyes are pale yellow.

photos.caption: Woodpigeon adult showing the distinctive white neck patches

life_stages.description: Young Woodpigeons lack the white neck patches entirely and are slightly duller brown-grey overall. They are often seen in summer following adults and begging for food. The white neck patches develop gradually through the first autumn.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both medium-large grey pigeons in similar habitats
similar_species.key_difference: Stock Dove is smaller and compact, with no white neck patches and no white wing bars. It has two small black wing bars instead. Frequents old trees with nest holes; less common than Woodpigeon.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both present year-round

photos.caption: Woodpigeon — the largest and most common UK pigeon

summary: One of the most ecologically important animals at Old Down — rabbits graze the chalk grassland short, which is exactly what rare wildflowers and butterflies need to survive. Without rabbits, coarser grasses would take over and the delicate chalk grassland plants would be smothered. Look for their warrens in the sunny slope banks.
full_description:
The Rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) was introduced to Britain by the Normans around 1100 AD and is now so thoroughly naturalised that it functions as a native species ecologically. At 40–50cm long, rabbits are easily recognised — brown-grey fur, long ears with black tips, large hind legs, and the distinctive white 'scut' (tail) that flashes as they flee. They are most active at dawn and dusk, though visible throughout the day at undisturbed sites like Old Down.

Rabbits are ecosystem engineers at Old Down. By grazing the chalk grassland very short and evenly, they prevent coarser, more competitive grasses from overwhelming the fine-leaved chalk grassland species that rare plants and butterflies depend on. Without rabbit grazing, the grassland at Old Down would gradually be colonised by rank grass, then Bramble and Hawthorn scrub, and the chalk grassland community — including Cowslip, Bird's-foot Trefoil, Small Blue butterfly, and Marbled White — would decline and eventually disappear. Myxomatosis can severely reduce rabbit populations, and when this happens the grassland quality changes noticeably within a few years.

Signs of rabbits are easy to find at Old Down. Warrens — networks of burrows — are visible as holes 10–20cm across with fresh-dug soil around the entrance, often on south-facing slopes where the chalk is near the surface. Round black droppings (about 1cm across) are scattered widely, often in latrine piles. Grazing marks on plants — clean-angled cuts on grass stems and shrub shoots — are also characteristic. Rabbits are important prey for Red Kite, Buzzard, Stoat, Fox, and Kestrel on the site.
native_info: Introduced to Britain by the Normans c.1100 AD. Now fully naturalised and one of the most widespread mammals in the UK. Most abundant on chalk, limestone, and sandy soils where burrowing is easy.
wildlife_value: Critical ecosystem engineer for chalk grassland — grazing maintains the short, diverse sward that rare plants and butterflies depend on at Old Down. Burrows provide shelter for other species including Rabbits obviously, but also Shelduck, Bumblebee queens, and various invertebrates. Major prey species for Red Kite, Buzzard, Kestrel, Fox, Stoat, and Weasel.

life_stages.description: Brown-grey fur above with pale buff underside; large ears 7–8cm long; powerful hind legs; white 'scut' (tail) that flashes when the animal runs. The white tail is a warning signal to other rabbits. Eyes are large and positioned on the sides of the head, giving a wide field of vision. Look for them in the early morning and evening, sitting up and alert before moving to feed.

photos.caption: Rabbit on chalk grassland — a key ecosystem engineer at Old Down
European Rabbit — brown-grey adult showing characteristic large ears
Rabbit showing alert posture and white tail (scut)

life_stages.description: Warrens are systems of interconnected burrows with entrance holes 10–20cm across, usually on sunny slopes or in hedgerow banks. Fresh soil (spoil) at the entrance indicates active use. Round dark droppings, about 1cm across, are scattered widely around the warren and in latrine piles on prominent spots. Gnawed grass and bark at ground level shows where rabbits have been feeding. Footprints show large hind feet landing in front of the smaller front feet.

Young rabbits (called kittens or kits) are born underground from February onwards and emerge at about 3 weeks old. They are miniature versions of adults but rounder, slightly fluffier, and with proportionally larger ears and eyes. Several litters are produced each year — rabbits can breed rapidly when conditions are good.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both medium-sized brown mammals with long ears in open grassland
similar_species.key_difference: Brown Hare is much larger (50–70cm), with longer black-tipped ears, longer hind legs, and a distinctly black-and-white tail (black on top, white below). Hares live entirely above ground — no warrens — and rely on speed. Hares have a wilder, more powerful look than Rabbits.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both present year-round; Hares are less common at Old Down than Rabbits

photos.caption: Rabbit — essential grazer of Old Down's chalk grassland
European Rabbit adult portrait
Rabbit showing the white scut (tail) that flashes as a warning signal

confidence_note: Buff-tailed Bumblebee can be confused with White-tailed Bumblebee (Bombus lucorum), which is very similar but has a cleaner white tail and brighter lemon-yellow bands. The tail colour — buff-orange vs white — is the key difference, but is not always easy to judge in the field.
summary: One of Britain's largest and most important bumblebees. The queen emerges in early spring — sometimes even in January in mild winters — and is enormous compared to other insects at that time of year. Watch Cowslips and Knapweed flowers at Old Down for the constant movement of workers collecting pollen and nectar.
full_description:
The Buff-tailed Bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) is one of the most abundant and widespread bumblebees in Britain. Queens are very large — up to 22mm long — with a yellow band on the thorax, a second yellow band on the abdomen, and a buff-orange tail. Workers are similar but smaller (11–17mm). Males are smaller still, with a more extensive yellow pattern and a yellow-tipped face. The tail colour varies and can be quite pale in worn individuals, making separation from the White-tailed Bumblebee tricky in the field.

Queen Buff-tailed Bumblebees are among the very first insects to emerge in spring, sometimes flying in January or February in mild weather. After hibernating in a small underground cell, the queen must feed intensively to build up energy reserves before finding a suitable nest site — typically an old mouse hole, compost heap, or underground cavity. She then builds a colony of 200–400 workers through spring and summer, which fan out to forage across a large area. A single worker will visit thousands of flowers per day.

At Old Down, Buff-tailed Bumblebees are among the key pollinators of Cowslip, Bird's-foot Trefoil, Knapweed, and Bramble. Their workers also visit Red Clover, Vetch species, and a wide range of other flowers. Other bumblebee species also occur at Old Down, including the Red-tailed Bumblebee (Bombus lapidarius) — unmistakable with an all-black body and red tail — and the Early Bumblebee (Bombus pratorum), which is smaller and has an orange tail even earlier in the year.
danger_note: Female bumblebees can sting if handled or if their nest is disturbed, but are not aggressive when foraging on flowers. Unlike honey bees, bumblebees can sting multiple times. Leave nests undisturbed.
native_info: Native throughout England, Wales, and southern Scotland. One of Britain's most common bumblebees, present in almost all habitats from gardens to chalk grassland. Colony size 200–400 workers.
wildlife_value: One of the most important pollinators in Britain, visiting a huge range of wildflowers. Essential for the pollination of Bramble, White Clover, Bird's-foot Trefoil, and many other plants at Old Down. The long-tongued workers can reach nectar in deeper flowers including Cowslip. Colonies provide food for Badgers who excavate nests for larvae and honeypot stores.

life_stages.description: The queen is the first sign of Buff-tailed Bumblebee in the year — a large, heavy bee appearing in February–April, flying low over the ground looking for a nest site, or feeding intensively on early flowers like Willowherb, Dandelion, and Blackthorn. She is noticeably larger than any worker bee. One yellow band on the thorax, one on the abdomen, and a buff-orange tail.

photos.caption: Buff-tailed Bumblebee queen foraging — note the large size and buff tail

life_stages.description: Workers are much smaller than the queen but share the same yellow-and-buff pattern. They visit flowers constantly, often carrying visible orange pollen baskets (corbiculae) on their hind legs. Watch a Knapweed or Bramble flower at Old Down and workers will pass through every few seconds on a warm day.

photos.caption: Buff-tailed Bumblebee worker on a flower

similar_species.similarity_note: Very similar species, often in the same habitat
similar_species.key_difference: White-tailed Bumblebee (Bombus lucorum) has a pure white tail (vs buff-orange), brighter lemon-yellow bands, and is generally slightly smaller. The difference in tail colour can be subtle in faded or worn individuals. Both species occur at Old Down.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both fly February–October

similar_species.similarity_note: Another common bumblebee at Old Down

confidence_note: Males are unmistakable — electric bright blue with black border and white fringe. Females are mostly brown with variable blue scales near the body and orange spots near the wing margin, and can be confused with Brown Argus or Small Blue females. Both sexes have diagnostic orange spots on the undersides of all wings.
summary: The male is an electric metallic blue that seems to glow in sunlight — one of the most beautiful sights of British grassland summer. Both sexes have lovely orange-spotted undersides. The caterpillars feed on Bird's-foot Trefoil, so finding the butterfly at Old Down means the chalk grassland is in good shape.
full_description:
The Common Blue (Polyommatus icarus) is the most widespread blue butterfly in Britain and among the most beautiful. Males have vivid sky-blue upperwings with a narrow black border and white fringe, and seem to glow in sunlight — a blue that is almost impossible to describe in writing. Females are predominantly brown with variable amounts of blue near the wing base and orange spots along the outer margins. Both sexes share the same distinctive underside: pale grey-buff with black spots and a row of vivid orange-red spots near the wing margins — this pattern is the reliable ID feature for both sexes.

The Common Blue has two broods at Old Down in a good year — the first flies May to June, the second July to September. The caterpillars feed primarily on Bird's-foot Trefoil (Lotus corniculatus), with some use of related legumes. Eggs are laid singly on the upper surface of trefoil leaflets. The caterpillars are green and well-camouflaged, and are tended by ants — the caterpillars have a special gland that produces a liquid the ants drink, and in return the ants protect the caterpillar from predators.

At Old Down, Common Blue is typically more numerous than Small Blue, and is a strong indicator of chalk grassland quality. On warm sunny days in July, it is possible to see males spiralling upward in territorial chases, females nectaring on Knapweed and Marjoram, and both sexes roosting with wings closed on tall grass stems in the evening.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. The most common and widespread blue butterfly in Britain. Most abundant on chalk and limestone grassland, coastal dunes, and brownfield sites where Bird's-foot Trefoil grows.
wildlife_value: Caterpillars are specifically dependent on Bird's-foot Trefoil, making this butterfly a reliable indicator of good chalk grassland. Caterpillars are tended by ants — a mutualistic relationship. Adults are prey for spiders and birds. The presence of Common Blue at Old Down indicates a healthy population of its food plant.

life_stages.description: Eggs are tiny, disc-shaped, and pale green-white, laid singly on the upper surface of Bird's-foot Trefoil leaflets. They are very difficult to spot without a hand lens. Newly hatched caterpillars eat the egg shell before starting on the leaf.

Green, slug-like caterpillar with a darker line along the back and pale sides — excellent camouflage on the trefoil leaves. Look for small black ants attending the caterpillar: the caterpillar has a gland on its back that produces a sweet secretion that ants drink, and the ants guard the caterpillar in return.

Electric sky-blue upperwings with a narrow black border and white fringe. The blue has a slightly violet tone in certain lights. Underwing is pale buff-grey with black spots and vivid orange spots near the margin. Males are territorial and can be seen chasing other males on sunny days.

Orange spots along the outer wing margin. The orange-spotted underside is the same as the male and is the most reliable identification feature.

summary: One of Britain's most abundant grassland butterflies, and one of the few that will fly on dull, overcast days. Old Down can be carpeted with Meadow Browns in July and August. The single large eye-spot on the forewing is the key ID feature.
full_description:
The Meadow Brown (Maniola jurtina) is Britain's most abundant butterfly by population, and one of the most characteristic species of summer grassland. Males are dark brown with a small orange patch on the forewing containing a single black eye-spot with a white centre. Females are larger with a more extensive orange-brown patch on the forewing and a more prominent eye-spot. The underside of the hindwing is mottled buff-brown with a small cluster of spots — much paler and less patterned than many browns.

The Meadow Brown is unusual among British butterflies in that it will fly in overcast and even light rain, unlike most species that only fly in sunshine. This makes it one of the most reliably visible butterflies on visits to Old Down through the summer. It is single-brooded — one flight period from June through September — and the adults live for several weeks, nectaring on Knapweed, Bramble, Marjoram, and many other flowers. The caterpillars feed on a range of fine grasses, which is why the species thrives in both chalk grassland and rough grassland habitats.

At Old Down, Meadow Brown is typically the most numerous butterfly by count in summer, often hundreds visible simultaneously on a warm July day. It makes an excellent species for children learning to count butterflies — it is abundant, easy to spot, and lands frequently on flowers. Look especially on Knapweed, Bramble flowers, and Ragwort.
native_info: Native throughout England, Wales, and Ireland. One of the most abundant butterflies in Britain. Found in almost all grassland habitats, from chalk downland to coastal dunes to roadside verges.
wildlife_value: Caterpillars feed on common fine grasses, making this butterfly independent of specialist plants and very adaptable. Adults are important pollinators of Knapweed, Bramble, and Marjoram. Prey for bats, spiders, and birds. The abundance of Meadow Brown at Old Down provides a baseline indicator for grassland quality that is easy to monitor.

life_stages.description: The caterpillar hibernates over winter as a small larva, resuming feeding in spring on fine grasses. It is green with a pale stripe along each side, well camouflaged in the grass stems. By May it has grown to full size and pupates in a chrysalis close to the ground.

Dark brown wings with a small orange-brown patch on the upper forewing and a single black eye-spot (with one or two white pupils). Males tend to be darker than females. The underside of the hindwing is mottled brown and buff — much plainer than the Gatekeeper.

photos.caption: Meadow Brown male showing the dark brown wings and eye-spot on forewing

life_stages.description: Females are slightly larger than males with a more extensive orange-brown band on the forewing and a more prominent eye-spot. The orange colouring makes females look warmer and brighter than males when settled on a flower. Both sexes rest with wings closed when not in active flight.

similar_species.key_difference: Gatekeeper (Pyronia tithonus) is smaller, with two white pupils in the eye-spot (Meadow Brown has one or two but usually one), more orange on the forewing, and a distinctly patterned underside of the hindwing (Meadow Brown's is plainer). Gatekeeper prefers scrub-grassland edges and hedgerows rather than open grassland.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Gatekeeper flies July–August; Meadow Brown June–September

similar_species.key_difference: Ringlet is darker brown, almost sooty, with multiple cream-ringed eyespots on the underside of both wings. Meadow Brown is warmer brown with much plainer hindwing underside.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Ringlet flies June–August; Meadow Brown June–September
